name: Kisspeptin-10
evidenceNote: Several small controlled human studies show kisspeptin-10 raises LH and testosterone for hours, mostly given by vein in a clinic. None ran longer than a few days or tested a clinical outcome, and the brain and desire studies used a different form, kisspeptin-54.
summary: Kisspeptin-10 is a short fragment of a reproductive hormone that raises LH in small human studies. It is unapproved and on FDA's compounding safety list.
keyTakeaway: Kisspeptin-10 is the smallest active piece of kisspeptin, the hormone that switches on the reproductive axis. In small studies of healthy men, an intravenous dose roughly tripled luteinizing hormone (LH) within 30 minutes, and longer infusions lifted testosterone. Healthy women in the early part of the cycle showed no response. No trial has tested it for fertility, libido, or low testosterone as a treatment. It is not FDA-approved, FDA has placed it in its compounding safety-risk category, and WADA bans it in male athletes.

blocks.text: Kisspeptins are a family of peptides cut from a single precursor protein made by the KISS1 gene. The longest natural form has 54 amino acids (kisspeptin-54). Kisspeptin-10 is the final ten amino acids of that chain, and it is the shortest piece that still fully activates the kisspeptin receptor [1].

Interest in the family took off after people born with faulty kisspeptin signaling were found to go through no puberty, which showed that the hormone is a required trigger for human reproduction [8]. Academic groups in the UK and elsewhere have since given kisspeptin-10 to volunteers to study how it shapes reproductive hormones. Outside research, it is sold online as an unregulated "research peptide," often marketed to men for testosterone and libido.

Kisspeptin acts upstream of the hormones most people know. It binds receptors on gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neurons in the hypothalamus, which then release GnRH in pulses. GnRH in turn prompts the pituitary to release LH and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), which drive the testes and ovaries [8]. In men, kisspeptin-10 increased both the number and the size of LH pulses, and a long infusion raised testosterone [1].

The response depends heavily on sex and timing. Healthy men responded at low doses, while healthy women in the follicular phase (the first half of the menstrual cycle) showed no hormone change even at much higher doses. Women in the days just before ovulation did respond [2]. Kisspeptin is also found in parts of the brain that handle emotion and sexual cues, which has led to research on desire and mood, though that work used kisspeptin-54 rather than kisspeptin-10 [6][7].

No. No kisspeptin product is approved for any use in the United States. FDA places kisspeptin-10 in Category 2 of its 503A bulk substance list, the group of compounding ingredients that raise significant safety concerns, and this listing was still in place in FDA's May 2026 update [9]. FDA's stated concern is a risk of immunogenicity (the body forming an immune response against the peptide) for some routes of use, along with little safety information for the routes proposed [10].
In sport, the 2026 WADA Prohibited List bans kisspeptin and its agonist analogs in males, under the testosterone-stimulating peptides in class S2.2.1, both in and out of competition [11].

Every published human study of kisspeptin-10 is small and short, and most gave it into a vein in a research unit. They show that the peptide moves reproductive hormones. They do not show that it treats any condition.

blocks.text: The better-known kisspeptin trials, including brain-scan studies in healthy men and a randomized crossover trial in 32 women with hypoactive sexual desire disorder (persistently low sexual desire that causes distress), gave kisspeptin-54 by infusion [6][7]. Those studies reported changes in brain activity during erotic images, not changes in sexual behavior, and they cannot be read across to a kisspeptin-10 injection bought online. A 2024 review from the field's leading group describes kisspeptin's therapeutic uses as still in development [8].

Two practical gaps matter when weighing online claims. First, the hormone effects in these studies came from carefully timed doses, mostly by vein, under supervision; how repeated self-injection over weeks behaves has not been reported. Second, more is not necessarily better: in the 2011 dose-response study, the highest bolus tested gave a smaller LH rise than the one below it [1].

Vials sold as kisspeptin-10 for "research use" are not made or tested under drug manufacturing rules, so their content, purity, and sterility are unknown. FDA's safety listing reflects exactly this gap: there is little information on what repeated injection of the compounded peptide does in people [10]. The published studies were run by endocrinology teams who measured hormones every few minutes, a very different setting from self-dosing at home.
